Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. - 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. - 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

items.content_html:

Roughly 75% of voters reflected Alberta's October 19th seperatist referendum. First Nations' opposition impacted the vote in some regions but it also extended beyond the ballot box. In this Yellowhead Brief, Michael Fabris examines how First Nations challenged separatism through strategic litigation and public mobilization, asserting that Alberta's future cannot be decided without addressing Indigenous jurisdiction and maintaining treaty relationships. That lesson extends to Alberta politics post-referundum.

items.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. Decades of deforestation and peatland drainage also left the landscape more vulnerable to ignition. The fires have spread hazardous haze across Indonesia and neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform, estimated that fires affected 2.88 million hectares from January through October. The Indonesian government had not confirmed that total or issued its own estimate. Researchers called for peatland restoration, stronger land protections and reduced fossil-fuel emissions. Fires were still burning, with smoke detected in eastern Kalimantan on Nov. 12.

items.title: [durhamradionews.com] Canada’s first small modular reactor faces delay and cost overrun
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Ontario Power Generation (OPG), the province-owned utility, says the first of four small modular reactors planned for the Darlington site east of Toronto will miss its October 2030 operating target and exceed its previously disclosed C$7.7 billion cost estimate. OPG has not yet provided a revised schedule or estimated the size of the overrun. It expects to substantially complete a cost-and-schedule assessment by mid-2027. The utility attributed the risks in part to unfinished engineering work on the first-of-its-kind BWRX-300 design, which it said is affecting construction and supply-chain performance. The four-reactor project has a C$20.9 billion budget. The first unit is the first small modular reactor to begin construction in a G7 country. OPG says construction continues while it works with reactor designer GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy to complete the outstanding engineering work.

items.title: [bbc.com] Brazil activates protective measures after about 20 isolated Awá approach
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [utilitydive.com] US orders Michigan coal plant to stay open despite court ruling
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The U.S. Energy Department issued a seventh emergency order requiring the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell coal plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, to keep operating for another 90 days, through mid-February 2027, despite a federal appeals court ruling in September that an earlier order was unlawful. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and maintain reliable electricity supplies; the department cited lessons from Winter Storm Fern and other events during the 2026 Arctic cold period. The plant had been scheduled to retire in May 2025. Michigan and other states, along with environmental groups, challenged the earlier orders, arguing there was no qualifying emergency. The appeals court agreed, and the Energy Department has asked the full court to rehear the case. That request remains pending as the new order takes effect.

items.title: [theguardian.com] EU proposes extra €45 billion Ukraine loan, faces fight over guarantees
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The European Commission proposed on Nov. 18 an additional €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027, covering about two-thirds of a projected €70 billion funding gap. It would supplement the €90 billion EU loan already approved for 2026 and 2027; the new package allocates up to €25 billion for military needs and €20 billion for Ukraine’s state budget. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the funding was intended to strengthen Kyiv’s position in negotiations with Russia. Ukraine would repay the principal only after receiving Russian reparations. The EU would raise the money on capital markets, with its common budget guaranteeing the borrowing. Budget support would be conditional on Ukrainian reforms, including on the rule of law and corruption. The Commission also wants other international partners to cover the remaining €25 billion of Ukraine’s estimated needs. Approval faces resistance from Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia, which have signalled they do not want to join the financing. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pressed for all 27 EU members to share responsibility and linked the Ukraine financing to talks on the bloc’s next long-term budget; Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico called that approach “blackmail”. EU leaders are due to discuss the proposal at a Brussels summit on Nov. 26-27, and the budget guarantee requires unanimous member-state backing.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items._excerpt: Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well (cbc.ca, nationalobserver.com). Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt (cbc.ca, thestar.com). For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027 (cbc.ca, thestar.com). The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing (boereport.com). Meta project: The Sturgeon County complex is a $13-billion, one-gigawatt development expected to come online in two to three years (cbc.ca). Cleanup backlog: The Orphan Well Association lists 7,328 wells awaiting decommissioning and 9,258 sites needing reclamation; it estimates cleanup costs for its inventory at $1.66 billion (cbc.ca, thestar.com). Emissions cap: Bill 42 would eliminate the oil-sands emissions cap, which set a 100-million-tonne limit and had never been enforced; emissions were about 84 million tonnes in 2023 (boereport.com). Public response: A September CBC-commissioned poll found 31% of Albertans strongly opposed data-centre development and another 26% mostly opposed it, with electricity bills and environmental effects among the concerns (cbc.ca).

items.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

France summoned Iran’s ambassador on Nov. 10 and said it would seek European Union sanctions and consider other responses to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration systems that Paris attributes to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Paris would take measures it considered proportionate to deter further attacks, including steps it would not disclose publicly. The Paris prosecutor’s office opened a judicial investigation into the Shahid Kaveh cyber unit and requested international arrest warrants for its leader and two deputies. items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Hackers use 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to steal continuous integration secrets
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A campaign dubbed wfx-loot used stolen credentials from 4,837 GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 repositories and plant code designed to steal developer and cloud secrets. Security researchers confirmed the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories. A separate analysis counted malicious commits in 8,093 public repositories, but that does not mean the code executed in each one. The attackers tested access with pull requests titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” then briefly inserted a roughly 1,500-line script into GitHub Actions workflows or npm installation hooks. The script sought GitHub, cloud, package-publishing and AI-service credentials. Attackers often reverted the changes and deleted workflow logs. The campaign relied on valid stolen account tokens, not a flaw in GitHub Actions. Researchers said the operation was still active on Nov. 12, with new probe requests and malicious code still appearing. They advised repository owners to revoke compromised access, rotate every secret available to affected workflows and check cloud accounts for persistent access.

items.title: [Fast Company] DOJ sues Lyft for allegedly denying rides to people with disabilities
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans With Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on ride-share services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”

Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for the treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one—or, in some cases, several—drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees, and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices, and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.

“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The Department of Justice said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

—By Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press

🪶 ✏️

A hands-on test by 少数派 on November 12 showed that the Home Assistant Connect AUX-2 plays music reliably in sync, but responds with a delay when starting playback and switching tracks. Nabu Casa’s €59 adapter connects older audio devices to the smart home. In the test, several speakers remained synchronized for hours after playback started; when creating or dissolving a group, the system responded more slowly than Apple’s AirPlay. The review recommends a wired network connection: playing lossless FLAC files over Wi-Fi may cause dropouts on heavily congested 2.4 GHz networks. The author suggests the Opus codec as an alternative, since it requires less bandwidth. The AUX-2 connects conventional speakers via Music Assistant and the open Sendspin protocol; passive speakers still require an amplifier.

items.title: [Macworld] How accurately does the Apple Watch measure your heart rate? We put it to the test
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Macworld

With the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, Apple introduced a new health-sensing system. The new energy-efficient LED sensors measure heart rate every five seconds. Heart rate variability is also measured significantly more frequently than before. Macwelt was able to verify this in our review of the Apple Watch Series 12. The watch now measures your pulse every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, and heart rate variability is now recorded every five minutes. The battery still lasts for 24 hours.

This is exciting, because the Apple Watch already had stellar heart-rate tracking. How often and how accurately has the Apple Watch been measuring key health parameters to date? Apple hides the answers to these questions in its support documents. For some measurements, there are no official figures at all. So we took a closer look using the Apple Watch Series 11, which has the same third-gen optical heart rate sensor that was introduced with the Apple Watch Series 6.

How often does the Apple Watch Series 11 measure heart rate?

The answer to this question depends on the situation and the settings on your Apple Watch. In workout mode, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five seconds. The watch also measures your heart rate at this high frequency for the first three minutes after your workout. However, there is also a special setting for long workouts, where the user can activate power-saving mode if required. Apple claims that measurements are taken less frequently in this mode. I recorded a HIIT workout using the Polar H10 chest strap as a reference device. I also started the same workout on the Apple Watch Series 11.

Foundry

The Apple Watch actually measures heart rate every five seconds while the wearer is exercising. Measurements in power-saving mode during a workout also take place every five seconds. However, the system pauses the measurement for several minutes. This means that the heart rate is measured in short intervals every 5 seconds, then the Apple Watch pauses. You can see this on the graph of the heart rates measured during the workout up to the green line: up to that point, the Apple Watch was running in power-saving mode; after that, I switched it off.

Speaking of power-saving mode. If this mode is activated all the time, no background measurements take place, neither of the heart rate nor of heart rate variability. Furthermore, the vital signs data following a recorded night’s sleep lacks the oxygen saturation readings from during the night.

The Apple Watch can also measure your heart rate every second, just like chest straps do during a workout. However, these measurements only occur sporadically: during user-initiated ECG readings and during background HRV measurements. When you launch the ECG app and place your finger on the Digital Crown, the animation on the Watch and the PDF generated afterwards show the heart rate readings for every second. During HRV measurement, too, the Apple Watch records each heart rate over the course of a minute and then uses a specific formula to calculate the time interval between individual heartbeats.

In the background, and particularly at night while you’re asleep, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate every five minutes. However, the measurements aren’t as regular as they are during exercise. The intervals can vary more significantly when you’re at rest.

I exported and analysed measurements from a sample night using the Health app. For the sake of clarity, the chart above shows only one hour. During six and a half hours of sleep, the Apple Watch took 83 measurements. The average interval between measurements here is 4 minutes 39 seconds, although gaps of 16 minutes or as little as 40 seconds are also possible.

How accurately does the Apple Watch measure heart rate data?

When unveiling the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple claimed that the new smartwatch was the most accurate heart rate fitness tracker on the market. While we can only verify this claim through a single test, older models show that the Apple Watch was already quite accurate when it came to heart rate measurement.

When we tested the Apple Watch Ultra 3, we found that the Ultra’s readings deviated only very slightly from those of the chest strap. I analysed the same HIIT workout described above using the Apple Watch Series 11. The following picture emerges from the progression of the two graphs. On average, the Apple Watch measures your heart rate quite accurately during exercise.

The correlation coefficient between the two measurements–from the Polar H10 and the Apple Watch Series 11–is 0.95. This means the Apple Watch measures quite closely to a chest strap. On average, the two readings differ by just one beat. However, there are outliers: the higher the heart rate, the less accurate the measurement becomes. This can be seen in the line showing heart rates of 160 beats per minute and above. The measurement is also rather inaccurate in power-saving mode, as the Apple Watch can completely miss heart rate spikes due to the sporadic mode.

The new features Apple announced for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 are exciting because they effectively turn the entire heart rate measurement algorithm on its head.
